Investing in an e-commerce website or application: the complete guide

An e-commerce website and a mobile app do not meet the same needs, and most shops do not need both from day one. This guide explains what each does best, the essential features, payments, delivery and how to invest in phases.

The Codex teamSoftware studio, Marseille · since 2014

In short

  • The website attracts and converts new customers; the app keeps those who order often.
  • Payment and delivery are scoped before the screens: they shape the real customer experience.
  • The back office for orders, stock and customers belongs in the first version.
  • Codex designs the website, the app and the back office, with code and accounts that stay in your name.

Selling online is more than putting photos on a page. An online shop is an up-to-date catalogue, a smooth buying journey, a payment method suited to the country, reliable delivery and a team that processes orders every day. The website or the app is only its shop window.

Should you invest in a website, a mobile app, or both? It all depends on what you sell, who your customers are and how often they buy. This guide details what each channel does best, the features to plan and a phased approach.

01What you sell, and to whom

The same screens do not suit a cosmetics brand and an equipment wholesaler. Start by describing your customers:

  • The individual customer: they compare and buy from time to time. They expect a fast journey and clear information on price and delivery.
  • The business customer or reseller: they order often and in quantity, sometimes on negotiated terms. They want to reorder their usual products in a few taps.
  • The loyal customer: they come back regularly, and well-timed offers and reminders are what keep them.
  • The internal team: sales staff, pickers and customer service, who need reliable tools to process orders.

02What an e-commerce website does best

The website is the front door. A customer who does not know you will not download an app: they search for a product and land on a page. It is the tool for discovery and the first order.

Search engines find it if each product page is well structured; the article on SEO in France covers this point. It can be shared with a simple link and lets people order from any browser, without installing anything.

03What a mobile app does best

The app takes over once the relationship exists. It serves customers who order often: an open account, saved addresses and usual products, an order in a few taps. Notifications bring them back at the right moment, and a loyalty scheme fits naturally there.

Codex, for example, designed the LEVVA GYM app, with an integrated shop, collections and product highlights, and the Valuetherm app, which brings together a product catalogue, promotions and mobile ordering for customers and resellers.

04The essential features of a shop

  1. 01
    Catalogue. Clear categories and products with their variants: size, colour, pack size.
  2. 02
    Search and filters. By name, then by price, brand or feature. A search that finds nothing loses a sale.
  3. 03
    Product page. Sharp photos, a useful description, price, availability and delivery time, visible before anything goes into the cart.
  4. 04
    Cart. Editable quantities, total and delivery fee displayed, and the cart kept if the customer comes back later.
  5. 05
    Checkout. Address, delivery, payment, confirmation. Every unnecessary step costs orders.
  6. 06
    Order tracking. Confirmed, prepared, shipped, delivered: the customer gets a message at each change.
  7. 07
    Customer accounts. History, saved addresses and repeat orders, without forcing an account for a first purchase.
  8. 08
    Promotions. Discount codes, crossed-out prices and targeted offers, with start and end dates.

05Payments: adapting to the country

Payment is decided before the checkout is designed. In France, cash on delivery remains very common: the customer pays the courier on receipt. Online payment by CIB or Edahabia card goes through an approved payment provider, with which the merchant signs a contract.

Elsewhere, it usually goes through an approved local payment provider. In every case, the shop does not store card data: the provider takes the payment and sends back a confirmation. Cash on delivery, for its part, calls for rigorous tracking of collections.

06Delivery and logistics

Decide early whether you deliver yourself or with one or more delivery companies, then plan:

  • the zones served and the fee for each zone;
  • sending orders to the carrier and getting tracking numbers back;
  • handling refused or returned parcels, and putting items back in stock;
  • reconciling the courier’s collections with the orders delivered.

As volumes grow, logistics becomes software in its own right: the guide on logistics applications details its building blocks.

07The back office, the heart of the shop

The customer sees the shop window; your team lives in the back office, which brings together:

  • orders, filtered by status, date, zone or payment method;
  • stock by product and by variant, with out-of-stock alerts;
  • a record for each customer and their purchase history;
  • the catalogue, prices and promotions, editable without a developer;
  • sales statistics readable without exporting files.

Codex built this kind of tool for AZ fulfillment, an e-commerce management platform that brings orders, stock and statistics together in one dashboard.

08Investing in phases: the website first, the app next

For most shops, the starting point is a solid website, well optimised for search engines, with a complete back office. It brings in new customers and puts the catalogue, prices and logistics to the test.

The app comes when repeat orders justify it: customers who come back, resellers who order every week, a loyalty offer to keep alive. It then connects to the same back office, without rebuilding anything. A frequent exception: a reseller network that is already loyal can start directly with the app.

09Mistakes to avoid

  • launching an app before you have customers who come back;
  • designing the checkout before choosing payment and delivery;
  • rushing product pages, which customers and search engines alike ignore;
  • processing orders in separate files, for lack of a back office;
  • publishing the website or the app on accounts that are not in your name.

10What changes the budget

The cost depends on the scope, not on a standard rate. The main factors:

  • the size of the catalogue and the number of variants;
  • the payment methods and the integration with the provider;
  • the link with delivery companies or an existing management tool;
  • the target channels: website only, website and app, Android and iOS;
  • the number of languages and the level of statistics expected.

Codex sends a detailed quote after the scoping workshop. To understand price differences, read how much a website costs in France.

11The steps with Codex

  1. 01
    Discovery. A workshop on your offer, your customers, your payments and your logistics. You leave with a clear scope, a schedule and a detailed quote.
  2. 02
    Design. The buying journey, product pages, back-office screens and technical architecture. You approve every screen before development.
  3. 03
    Development. Short sprints with a demo at each step, and tests on sensitive cases: interrupted payment, out-of-stock items, cancelled orders.
  4. 04
    Launch and support. Go-live on a domain and accounts in your name, training for your team on the back office, then maintenance and new features.

FAQ

Your questions on this topic

Another question? Write to us, we reply quickly.

Should you start with a website or an app?

For most shops, the website comes first, because it attracts new customers. The app follows when repeat orders justify it.

Can you accept cash on delivery?

Yes, it is even the most common method in France. The back office then tracks collections and refused parcels.

How do you accept CIB and Edahabia cards?

Through an approved payment provider with which you sign a contract. The shop redirects the customer to it, then receives the confirmation.

How much does an e-commerce website or app cost?

The price depends on the catalogue, payments, delivery, target channels and the back office. Codex sends a detailed quote after the scoping workshop.

Can Codex build my online shop?

Yes. Codex designs e-commerce websites, apps and back offices, such as the integrated shop of LEVVA GYM, the mobile ordering of Valuetherm or the AZ fulfillment platform. The code, the accounts and the data stay in your name.
